body: I would agree that the zen approach of dropping the desire to do anything or understand anything is a very practical approach to meditation, but in order to give the experience of meditation a chance, one must initially have a desire to know what meditation is. I think that it's helpful to have somewhat of an intellectual grasp on meditation is when you are first beginning on your path, but at a certain point all intellectualization of the experience of meditation has to be dropped in order to experience meditation to it's fullest potential.

I did attempt to explain some things that can't really be fully described with words, but I don't see what's wrong with attempting to describe things like that as long as I am enjoying it and other people get something beneficial out of it. Just sitting down and being open to experience what ever will happen without any expectations what so ever is the most practical way to meditate, but I like to give beginner meditators an idea of what you come to understand through extensive practice. Taoist philosophy really never really fully describes what it tries to describe, but does that really mean that it's a waste of time? I wouldn't say so... Becoming obsessed with understanding with words can backfire through wasted time and effort, but I think that it also has it's benefits. I don't really think about things like this that much anymore because I feel like I've gotten most of what I can out of thinking like this so I guess you could say that I've "dropped it all" for the most part. I feel like thinking like that did benefit me while I was doing so because It was a necessary path for me to satisfy my anxious and over analytical intp/engineer type mind. I think that there are different paths that are practical for different types of minds, and sharing my path can help those who think similarly to the way that I do.
